notes.short: The arrow of victory and the ground struck thrice
notes.about: The dying Elisha has King Jehoash shoot an arrow out the east window, the prophet's hands on the king's, and calls it “the LORD’s arrow of victory” over Aram. Told to strike the ground, the king strikes only three times, and Elisha says he will now defeat Aram only three times.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.means: the victory the LORD would give over Aram at Aphek; the arrows then struck to the ground stood for the number of victories

notes.evidence: Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a symbolical act showing the promised victories, the arrows shot down a token of their number. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the arrow a symbol of the Lord's help, the shooting of Aram's overthrow. Adam Clarke calls it all emblems of Israel's deliverance. George Rawlinson (Barnes' Notes) says the shooting typified the victories.

cites.quote: Elisha directed Joash to do this, as a symbolical act, designed to intimate more fully and significantly the victories promised to the king of Israel over the Syrians. ... His shooting the other arrows into the ground was in token of the number of victories he was taken to gain; but his stopping at the third betrayed the weakness of his faith
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He then placed his hands upon the king's hands, as a sign that the power which was to be given to the bow-shot came from the Lord through the mediation of the prophet. ... The arrow that was shot off was to be a symbol of the help of the Lord against the Syrians to their destruction. ... The shooting of the arrows to the earth was intended to symbolize the overthrow of the Syrians.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Take bow and arrows - The bow, the arrows, and the smiting on the ground, were all emblematical things, indicative of the deliverance of Israel from Syria.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Elisha put his hands upon the king's hands - A symbolic act, indicating that the successes, which the shooting typified, were to come, not from human skill, or strength, or daring, but from the presence and the power of God.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jehoash answers with a fable of thistle and cedar
notes.about: Amaziah of Judah, proud after defeating Edom, challenges Jehoash of Israel to battle. Jehoash answers with a fable: a thistle asks a cedar for its daughter as a bride for its son, and a wild beast tramples the thistle. Verse 10 applies it to Amaziah's pride. Chronicles tells it again.

figure.name: Apologue
figure.words: A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon
figure.means: a man who rates himself above his strength, as Amaziah did against stronger Israel; the beast that tramples it is the sudden fall that pride brings

notes.evidence: Robert Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it an admonitory fable on the effects of pride and ambition. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) likens it to Jotham's fable: the thornbush pictures a proud man overrating his strength. Adam Clarke calls it a parable, the thistle Amaziah and the cedar Jehoash. C. J. Ball (Ellicott) calls it a pithy parable contrasting the two kingdoms' strength.
notes.limit: The writers differ on how closely to apply it. Some take the thistle as Amaziah, the cedar as Jehoash and the beast as Israel's army; others say it pictures any proud man and his sudden fall, without pressing each point.

cites.quote: This was the design of the admonitory fable related by Joash in his reply. The thistle, a low shrub, might be chosen to represent Amaziah, a petty prince; the cedar, the powerful sovereign of Israel ... the parable may be explained generally, as describing in a striking manner the effects of pride and ambition
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Jehoash (Joash) answered his insolent challenge ... with a similar fable to that with which Jotham had once instructed his fellow-citizens ( Jdg 9:8 .). ... the thorn-bush putting itself upon an equality with the cedar is a figurative representation of a proud man overrating his strength ... The trampling down of the thorn-bush by a wild beast is only meant to set forth the sudden overthrow
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The meaning of this parable is plain. The thistle that was in Lebanon - Amaziah, king of Judah, sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon - Jehoash, king of Israel ... And there passed by a wild beast - Jehoash and his enraged army, and trode down the thistle - utterly discomfited Amaziah and his troops
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: It is obvious to compare with this brief but most pithy parable that of Jotham ( Jdg 9:8-15 ). The contrast between the northern and southern kingdoms in point of military strength and resources, and the disdainful tolerance with which the former regarded the latter, could hardly have found more forcible expression.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Climbed and then felled; dug and then dried up
notes.about: The boast in these two verses is built the same way. In each, the second half gives the result of the first, what the king of Assyria meant to do next: having climbed the peaks of Lebanon, he cuts down its cedars; having dug wells and drunk foreign waters, he dries up the streams of Egypt.

lines.words: With my many chariots I have ascended to the heights of the mountains, to the remote peaks of Lebanon.
I have cut down its tallest cedars, the finest of its cypresses. I have reached its farthest outposts, the densest of its forests.
I have dug wells and drunk foreign waters.
With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the two verses are kept quite uniform, the second half of each giving the result of the first, what the Assyrian meant to do further once the first was done: having climbed the heights of Lebanon he lays waste its trees, and the drying up of the streams of Egypt follows from digging wells in the desert.
notes.limit: The note is about how the boast is set out, not about which of these deeds the king had already done.

cites.quote: The two verses are kept quite uniform, the second hemistich in both cases expressing the result of the first ... When he has ascended the heights of Lebanon, he devastates the glorious trees of the mountain. Consequently in Kg2 19:24 the drying up of the Nile of Egypt is to be taken as the result of the digging of wells in the parched desert
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)
